headline: Nothing Ear (3a): record calls and audio snapshots for under $100
summary: The new sub-$100 earbuds feature 'Audio Snapshot' to record quick audio moments and can capture up to two hours of calls and meetings.
details: Nothing has unveiled its latest wireless earbuds, the Ear (3a), positioned between the Ear (a) and Ear (3). These budget-friendly buds are priced under $100 and come in striking pink and yellow colorways, alongside the standard black and white.

The standout feature is 'Audio Snapshot,' allowing users to record short audio clips directly on the earbuds using their 32MB of built-in storage. These recordings, triggered by pinching both earbuds, capture audio from just before and after the press and sync to the Nothing X app for editing, sharing, and transcription.

Beyond personal audio notes, the Ear (3a) can record up to two hours of calls and meetings. For privacy, participants will be notified when a recording is active. The Nothing X app also allows users to create shareable 'quote cards' from transcribed moments.

Audio quality is enhanced with a new 12mm dynamic driver for deeper bass and improved detail, supporting LDAC streaming and an 8-band EQ. The earbuds also feature spatial audio for a more immersive listening experience.

Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) is present, rated up to 45 dB, with Nothing claiming a 17.1 percent improvement over previous models due to algorithm and acoustic mesh enhancements, covering a broader frequency range.
Battery life offers up to 42 hours of total listening time with the charging case. The buds alone provide up to 10 hours without ANC, dropping to 25 hours with ANC enabled.
caption:

headline_marked: Modder builds [[8,192-core RISC-V GPU]] with 2,000W+ power draw
headline: Modder builds 8,192-core RISC-V GPU with 2,000W+ power draw
summary: A hardware hacker created a custom graphics card using thousands of microcontrollers, resulting in a massive power consumption of over 2,000 watts.
details: Hardware hacker Matthias Balwierz, known as Bitluni, has constructed a unique graphics card featuring 8,192 RISC-V microcontrollers. This ambitious project effectively combines a GPU with a display, as each microcontroller is directly soldered with an RGB LED.

The goal was to achieve a resolution of 320x200, requiring approximately 64,000 chips in total. For this initial stage, Balwierz used 8,192 chips, creating boards with 16x32 'pixels' arranged in a circular pattern.

The most striking specification is the power draw, which reaches a staggering 2,161 watts. This immense power requirement is met by a Corsair WS3000 ATX power supply unit and custom voltage converters.
Each microcontroller used is a QingKe CH570 RISC-V unit, costing about $0.13 each. The final project, with the full 320x200 array, is estimated to cost over $8,000 in chips alone.

Balwierz custom-designed all PCBs, power delivery circuits, and interface boards. He even developed a 3D-printed tool, attached to a 3D printer, to program each individual microcontroller with precision.
